description: Just some casual college students who love space and computers
summary: Project AlienX lets anyone search real NASA SPHEREx infrared images for things that move. Enter a star name or sky coordinates, and our tool downloads every SPHEREx observation of that patch from NASA’s IRSA archive, aligns them, and plays them like a little video. You can scroll or drag a time slider through the dates, blink between epochs, and watch the sky change. Difference imaging then subtracts the sky: fixed stars vanish and only what moved or changed remains. A detection pipeline classifies every change (asteroid, high-proper-motion star, variable star or artifact) and checks known asteroids and catalogs. We tested it on the challenge targets: for Barnard’s Star it measured 10.50 ± 0.43″/yr against a catalog value of 10.39″/yr. A vision-language model we fine-tuned on epoch pairs, plus a grounded analysis engine, explains what you are seeing. The tool makes NASA’s newest all-sky survey explorable by students and citizen scientists, and it is the same method astronomers use to hunt for a distant Planet X.
details:
What it does
Project AlienX turns NASA SPHEREx data into an interactive “little video” of any patch of sky. Users enter a star name (e.g. Barnard’s Star) or RA/Dec coordinates; the tool fetches every SPHEREx observation of that field and plays them in time order, so moving and changing objects are easy to spot.

How it works

  1. Data: real SPHEREx images are fetched from NASA/IPAC IRSA (Simple Image Access and cutout services), using all available epochs and the best-suited wavelength band (e.g. the longest band for cold brown dwarfs like WISE 0855).
  2. Alignment: images are reprojected onto one coordinate grid using their WCS, with the same brightness stretch.
  3. Time exploration: a scroll-driven viewer and a time slider move through the epochs, with real dates shown (“observed”) and positions between dates labelled “interpolated”. Blink, play/loop and frame-stepping are included.
  4. Difference imaging: the latest image minus the earliest. Fixed stars cancel; whatever moved or changed lights up.
  5. Detection and classification: every change is detected and classed as an asteroid (cross-checked with IMCCE SkyBoT and JPL SB Ident), a proper-motion star, a known variable, a single-image transient or an artifact. Saturated stars are measured from their PSF wings, not rejected.
  6. Target lock: named objects are resolved with SIMBAD, and their positions are propagated with proper motion and parallax to each observation date, so the tool always tracks the object the user asked for.
  7. AI analyst: a Qwen2.5-VL-7B vision-language model we fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,000 labelled epoch-pair images classifies the change. Answers are always paired with the measured numbers, and unverified model text is labelled as such.

Results on the challenge targets

  • Barnard’s Star: 10.50 ± 0.43″/yr measured vs 10.39″/yr catalog, direction matching within 2°
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.91 ± 0.28″/yr vs 4.68″/yr, treated as an unresolved brown-dwarf pair
  • WISE 0855−0714: detected at 4.4–5.0 µm, 6.8 ± 2.4″/yr vs 8.15″/yr
  • RW Aurigae: brightness change of 0.58 mag at 12σ
  • R Draconis: core saturated in all epochs, so variability is reported as inconclusive rather than over-claimed

In the fields searched we found no Planet X-like slow mover, and the tool reports its search depth (about AB 17.8) and area honestly.

Benefits and impact
It makes SPHEREx’s repeated all-sky coverage explorable without coding, gives students and citizen scientists a hands-on way to see parallax, proper motion and variability, and applies the real technique used in searches for distant Solar System bodies.

Tools
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion; Python with astropy, reproject, numpy and scipy; Unsloth, Hugging Face Transformers/TRL and Qwen2.5-VL; FastAPI; Google Cloud; Cloudflare Tunnel.

Creativity and design choices
Scroll-driven storytelling, honest uncertainty labels (“observed” vs “interpolated”, “unconfirmed”, “inconclusive”), a pipeline-test mode that injects a synthetic Planet X to prove the search would catch one, and a fallback analyst so the site still works if the AI server is offline.
